title: Transformations and Jacobians
breadcrumb: Probability → Transformations → Functions of random variables
engineName: Probability — the distribution of something built from other variables
objectives: Choose between the cdf route, the Jacobian route and the conditional-ratio route.
Compute a Jacobian determinant and say why the density is multiplied by it.
Derive that X | X + Y = s is Uniform(0, s) and explain where the rate cancels.
Give the sum as Gamma(n, λ) and the minimum as exponential(nλ) without confusing them.
Condition Poisson counts on a total to get a binomial, and binomials to get a hypergeometric.
Apply memorylessness correctly, including the exponent.

prereq.name: The exponential and Gamma distributions
prereq.why: Nearly every example is built from exponentials, and the Gamma is what their sums become.

prereq.name: Joint densities and independence
prereq.why: The method starts from a joint density, and independence is what makes it a product.

prereq.name: Conditional densities
prereq.why: June 2026's question is a conditional density written as a ratio, which is the quickest of the three routes.

prereq.name: Partial derivatives and determinants
prereq.why: The Jacobian is a determinant of partial derivatives, and the lesson computes several.

traps: X | X + Y = s is Uniform(0, s), NOT Gamma(2, λ) — the Gamma is the distribution of the SUM.
The sum of n exponentials is Gamma(n, λ); the MINIMUM is exponential(nλ). Do not swap them.
The minimum has rate nλ, not λ/n — it arrives sooner, not later.
E(X | X + Y = s) = s/2, not 1/λ; the conditional answer must contain s and not λ.
Two binomials given their total give a HYPERGEOMETRIC, not a binomial.
In P(T > 6 | T > 4) with rate 2, the exponent is 2 × 2 = 4, not 2 or 6.
The Jacobian formula needs the map to be one-to-one; Y = X² needs both branches.
A conditional-given-the-total answer containing the rate has failed to cancel something.

sheet: Three routes: cdf method for minima and maxima; conditional ratio for a sum; Jacobian in general.
Jacobian: f_{U,V}(u,v) = f_{X,Y}(x,y)·|det ∂(x,y)/∂(u,v)|, the determinant being the area-scaling factor.
For (U,V) = (X, X+Y): x = u, y = v−u, Jacobian = det[[1,0],[−1,1]] = 1, so the density transfers unchanged.
June 2026 Q25: f(x | X+Y = s) = λ²e^(−λs)/(λ²s e^(−λs)) = 1/s on (0,s), so X | X+Y = s ~ Uniform(0,s).
At s = 2 that is Uniform(0,2) — option C. The marked Gamma(2,λ) is the distribution of the SUM.
The rate λ cancels entirely, so the answer does not depend on how fast the process runs.
Verified: 5,397 draws conditioned near X+Y = 2 gave mean 1.0051, sd 0.5772 (against 2/√12 = 0.5774), KS p = 0.230.
E(X | X+Y = s) = s/2. Check by the tower property: E((X+Y)/2) = (2/λ)/2 = 1/λ = E(X) ✓.
Sum of n iid exponential(λ) ~ Gamma(n, λ): mean n/λ, variance n/λ², skewness 2/√n.
Minimum of n iid exponential(λ) ~ exponential(nλ): mean 1/(nλ). Simulated at λ=1.5: 0.2217 for n=3 against 0.2222.
X/(X+Y) ~ Uniform(0,1) for two iid exponentials. Simulated mean 0.49992, variance 0.08341 against 1/12.
2λX ~ χ² with 2 df, since λX ~ exponential(1) = Gamma(1,1) and doubling gives scale 2. Simulated mean 1.998, variance 4.005.
Poisson split: N₁ | N₁+N₂ = k ~ Binomial(k, μ₁/(μ₁+μ₂)). Rates λ and 2λ give p = 1/3, free of λ and of t.
Binomial split: X | X+Y = k ~ Hypergeometric(m+n, m, k), free of p — the basis of Fisher's exact test.
Memorylessness: P(T > s+t | T > s) = P(T > t). Rate 2 gives P(T>6|T>4) = e^(−4) = 0.018316.
Poisson process: given exactly one event in an interval, its position is uniform; given k, the positions are k sorted uniforms.
Beta from Gammas: U/(U+V) ~ Beta(a,b) independent of U+V ~ Gamma(a+b, λ); a = b = 1 gives the uniform result.
cards: X | X + Y = s, iid exponentials
s/2, with no λ in it
One Poisson event in an interval
Its position is uniform on the interval
Beta(a, b), independent of the sum
tricks: Minimum or maximum? Use survival functions and multiply — one line.
Conditional on a sum? Write f(x, s−x)/f_sum(s) — also one line.
Anything else? Jacobian, then integrate out the variable you did not want.
Check a 'given the total' answer for the rate: if λ or p survives, something did not cancel.
Check a conditional expectation contains the conditioning value: s/2 not 1/λ.
For memorylessness, the exponent is the rate times the REMAINING time, not the total.
shortcuts: (x, x+y) has unit Jacobian, so the joint density needs no adjustment at all.
Gamma skewness is 2/√n, so the normal approximation improves at a visible rate: 2, 1.41, 0.89, 0.63, 0.37 for n = 1, 2, 5, 10, 30.
32/81 = 0.3951 and e^(−4) = 0.0183 are the two numerical answers in this topic's variants.
remember: Given the total, the split is uniform.
Sum is Gamma; minimum is exponential with rate nλ.
If the rate survives a conditioning, you made an error.

howto: Section 5 is June 2026's question and the whole lesson in miniature: the joint density of two independent exponentials depends on x and y only through their sum, so along a line of fixed sum it is constant, and the conditional distribution is therefore flat. Read the cancellation step carefully — both λ² factors and both exponentials disappear, which is why the answer contains no rate, and that absence is a useful check on any question of this kind. Section 3's chart is worth a minute: raise the number of exponentials being added and watch Gamma(n, λ) form a peak and approach a normal, with the skewness 2/√n reported so the rate of convergence is visible rather than asserted. Section 7 generalises the conditioning device to Poisson and binomial counts, where the rate and the success probability cancel in just the same way — and that is the idea behind Fisher's exact test. If short of time, sections 3, 4, 5 and 8 are the lesson. The optional section states the Jacobian theorem properly, derives the Beta from two Gammas, and warns about the one-to-one requirement that Y = X² violates.

provenance: Authored November 2026 on June 2026 Q25 (answered wrongly, marked D against C): X and Y independent exponential(λ), find the conditional distribution of X given X + Y = 2. The conditional density is f(x, s−x)/f_{X+Y}(s) = λ²e^(−λs)/(λ²s e^(−λs)) = 1/s on (0, s), so X | X+Y = s is Uniform(0, s) and the answer is Uniform(0, 2); the marked Gamma(2, λ) is the distribution of the SUM. The striking feature, taught as the lesson's organising idea, is that λ cancels completely — the joint density of independent exponentials depends on x and y only through their sum, so it is constant along any line of fixed sum. Verified by simulation: 600,000 pairs at λ = 1.5, of which 5,397 were kept near X+Y = 2, gave mean 1.0051 against 1, sd 0.5772 against 2/√12 = 0.5774, deciles matching Uniform(0,2) throughout, and a Kolmogorov–Smirnov p-value of 0.230. All nine variants are taught in named sections and pooled, including the Poisson interarrival item retagged into Q25 from the maths variant file earlier in this project, which belongs here because memorylessness is what makes the conditional uniform. Every other figure was computed and simulated: X/(X+Y) ~ Uniform(0,1) (mean 0.49992, variance 0.08341 against 1/12, KS p = 0.890); sums as Gamma(n, λ) at n = 1, 2, 5, 10; minima as exponential(nλ) at n = 3 and 7; 2λX ~ χ²₂ (mean 1.9984, variance 4.0045, KS p = 0.101); the Poisson split P(N₁ = 1 | total = 4) = 32/81 = 0.39506 against a simulated 0.39459 over 101,098 qualifying draws; and the binomial-given-total hypergeometric at m = 6, n = 4, k = 3 (empirical 0.0327, 0.3003, 0.4991, 0.1680 against the exact 0.0333, 0.3000, 0.5000, 0.1667). The memorylessness figure needed a second attempt: conditioning 600,000 draws on T > 4 retained only 205, so the estimate 0.0253 against the exact e^(−4) = 0.018316 was pure sampling error; simulating the shifted variable over four million draws gave 0.018388, confirming the formula. Introduces the `gamma-sum` visualisation, written for this lesson and reusable for 1.6 and 1.9; its means, variances and the skewness 2/√n were checked against the simulated values and its densities integrate to 1.00000000. Previous-year questions are stored separately and carry their exam cycle.

scenes.title: Before the lesson — four things it will assume
scenes.objective: Fix the exponential's basic facts and the mechanics of changing variables.

ask.q: You know the joint density of (X, Y) and you want the density of X + Y. What is the obstacle?
ask.nudge: A density is a function of as many variables as you have. One sum is one variable — what happened to the other?

body: This topic asks for the distribution of something built out of other random variables: a sum, a ratio, a minimum, a scaling. There are three standard routes and the lesson uses all three.

The cdf route works directly on P(g(X) ≤ t) and is best for minima and maxima. The Jacobian route changes variables in the joint density and is the general method. The third route is the one June 2026 used: write a CONDITIONAL density as a ratio, which is a change of variables in disguise.

The obstacle in the question above is that a single sum is one variable where there were two, so you cannot change variables with it alone. The fix is to introduce a second, convenient variable — here U = X and V = X + Y — transform, and then integrate out or condition on whichever one is not wanted.
Four checks before starting.

items.ask: For an exponential with rate λ, give the density, the cdf and the mean.
items.recall: f(x) = λe^(−λx) for x ≥ 0; F(x) = 1 − e^(−λx); mean 1/λ, variance 1/λ².
refresh: Mind the parameterisation: 'rate λ' gives mean 1/λ, while 'mean θ' gives density (1/θ)e^(−x/θ). Exam options usually make clear which, and the mean distinguishes them.
The survival function e^(−λx) is the useful form, because every minimum and every memorylessness calculation is a product of survival probabilities.
Two independent exponentials have joint density λ²e^(−λ(x+y)), which depends on x and y only through their SUM — the single fact behind this whole lesson.

items.ask: What is the distribution of the sum of n independent exponential(λ) variables?
items.recall: Gamma(n, λ), with mean n/λ and variance n/λ².
refresh: The Gamma's shape parameter counts how many exponentials went in, which is why waiting for the nᵗʰ event of a Poisson process is Gamma-distributed.
Checked by simulation at λ = 1.5: for n = 1, 2, 5, 10 the sample means were 0.667, 1.336, 3.329, 6.671 against the exact 0.667, 1.333, 3.333, 6.667.
A practice variant asks this directly, with 'exponential(nλ)' as the trap — that is the MINIMUM, not the sum.

items.ask: State the Jacobian method for a change of variables.
items.recall: If (U, V) = g(X, Y) is one-to-one, then f(u,v) = f(x,y) · |∂(x,y)/∂(u,v)|, with x and y written in terms of u and v.
refresh: The Jacobian determinant is the local area-scaling factor. It appears because a density is a per-unit-area quantity, so stretching the plane dilutes it.

For the transformation used throughout this lesson, U = X and V = X + Y, the inverse is x = u, y = v − u, and the Jacobian determinant is the determinant of [[1, 0], [−1, 1]], which is 1. So the joint density transfers unchanged — the reason the algebra stays clean.
The method needs the map to be one-to-one on the region of interest; otherwise split the region into pieces where it is.

items.ask: Which continuous distribution is memoryless, and what does that mean?
items.recall: The exponential, uniquely: P(T > s + t | T > s) = P(T > t).
refresh: For a Poisson process with rate 2 per minute, P(T > 6 | T > 4) = P(T > 2) = e^(−4) = 0.018316 — a practice variant. The elapsed four minutes are simply forgotten.
Equivalently the hazard rate is constant. Lesson 1.5 showed the geometric is the discrete counterpart and the only discrete law with the property.

Memorylessness is what makes this lesson's central result work: because the exponential has no memory, knowing the TOTAL X + Y tells you nothing about which part of it X occupies, so X is uniform across it.

scenes.title: Knowing the total says nothing about the split
scenes.objective: See why the conditional distribution comes out flat, before the algebra.
body: Two independent exponential waiting times add to 2 minutes. Where in that interval did the first one end?

The answer is: anywhere, with equal probability. The conditional distribution of X given X + Y = 2 is Uniform(0, 2), so the first waiting time is as likely to have taken 0.1 minutes as 1.0 or 1.9. The intuition that it 'should' be concentrated near the middle, or near zero, is simply wrong.

The reason is visible in the joint density. Two independent exponentials have joint density λ²e^(−λ(x+y)), which depends on x and y ONLY through their sum. So along the line x + y = 2 the density is constant, and conditioning on that line produces a flat distribution. No calculation is needed to see it — only the observation that the joint density is a function of the sum alone.

Notice what cancels: the rate λ disappears entirely. A fast process and a slow one give the same answer, because conditioning on the total has already absorbed everything the rate controls. That is the kind of result worth remembering as a fact rather than re-deriving under exam pressure.

scenario.teaser: A fault is known to have occurred during a two-hour window, and an engineer searches the middle first.
scenario.title: Where in the interval did it happen?
body: A monitoring system records that exactly one fault occurred during a two-hour window but not when. An engineer, reasoning that faults 'tend to cluster around the middle of a period', begins examining logs from the central portion.

If faults arrive as a Poisson process, that reasoning is wrong in a specific and useful way: given that exactly one event occurred in an interval, its time is UNIFORM over that interval. There is no central tendency to exploit, and the first and last minutes are as likely as any other.

This is the same fact as the lesson's main result, seen from the other side. The waiting time to the fault and the waiting time from the fault to the end of the window are the two exponential pieces, and conditioning on their total being two hours makes the split uniform.

The practical consequence is a change of search strategy rather than a correction to it. With no informative prior over position, the efficient approach is a systematic sweep or a bisection of the log, not a guess at the middle. And if the search is costly, the expected cost is the same wherever one starts — which is itself worth knowing, because it means effort should go into making each check cheaper rather than into choosing where to begin.

The result also generalises in a way worth carrying: given that exactly k events occurred in an interval, their times behave like k independent uniform draws on that interval, sorted. So with three faults in the window, their positions are the order statistics of three uniforms — which is lesson 1.1's material, and gives expected positions at 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4 of the way through.

What makes all of this work is memorylessness. A process with wear-out, where faults become more likely as equipment ages, would NOT give a uniform position, and the engineer's instinct could then be right. The uniformity is a consequence of the exponential assumption, not a general truth about intervals.
scenario.q: Why does the engineer's search strategy gain nothing from guessing the middle?
scenario.answer: Because for a Poisson process, given that exactly one event occurred in an interval, its position is uniform over that interval — every moment is equally likely, so there is no region of higher probability to search first. This follows from the same conditioning that makes X | X + Y = s uniform on (0, s): the joint density of the two exponential pieces depends only on their sum, so it is constant along the line where the sum is fixed. The instinct would only be right for a process whose hazard rises with time, which an exponential's by definition does not.

ask.q: The rate λ cancelled out of the answer entirely. What does that tell you about how much the conditional distribution depends on how fast the process runs?
ask.nudge: If you were told the total was 2 minutes, would knowing whether the process is fast or slow change where the split fell?

scenes.title: Watch exponentials add up to a Gamma
scenes.objective: See the shape parameter count the exponentials, and the normal appear.

viz.caption: The density of a sum of n independent exponential(λ) variables, which is Gamma(n, λ), with a normal curve of the same mean and variance shown from n = 2 onwards.

body: Start at n = 1. The sum of one exponential is that exponential: the density is highest at zero and decays, with skewness 2 and no interior peak.

Step to n = 2 — the case June 2026's question uses. A peak appears away from the origin, and the density at zero drops to zero. Gamma(2, λ) is the distribution of X + Y, which is what the marked answer gave; the question asked for X GIVEN that sum, which is a different object entirely.

Keep raising n and watch two things at once. The mean n/λ and the variance n/λ² both grow linearly, so the curve slides right and widens — but the RELATIVE spread sd/mean = 1/√n shrinks, which is why the shape tightens in proportion.

The skewness readout is 2/√n: 2 at n = 1, 1.41 at n = 2, 0.89 at n = 5, 0.63 at n = 10, 0.37 at n = 30. The teal normal curve converges on the Gamma at exactly that rate — the central limit theorem arriving, with its speed shown on a slider.
Change λ at fixed n and note what does NOT change: the skewness. The rate rescales the horizontal axis and nothing else, because λ is a scale parameter. Only the shape parameter n changes the shape.

ask.q: The skewness is 2/√n regardless of λ. Why does changing the rate leave the shape untouched?
ask.nudge: If S ~ Gamma(n, λ), what is the distribution of λS? Which parameter survives that rescaling?

scenes.title: Three routes, and the transformation that does the work
scenes.objective: Know the general method and the specific one this topic keeps using.

blocks.body:
For a single function of several variables, work on the cdf directly.
    P(min > t) = P(all > t) = ∏P(Xᵢ > t) = e^(−nλt)  for iid exponential(λ),
so the minimum is exponential with rate nλ and mean 1/(nλ) — a practice variant, and the trap is to answer exponential(λ/n). Simulated at λ = 1.5: the minimum of 3 had mean 0.2217 against the exact 0.2222, and of 7 had 0.0952 against 0.0952.

For a one-to-one map (U, V) = g(X, Y):
    f_{U,V}(u,v) = f_{X,Y}(x, y) · |∂(x,y)/∂(u,v)|,
with x and y expressed through u and v. Then integrate out whichever variable is not wanted. The Jacobian is the area-scaling factor, and it appears because densities are per-unit-area.

Take U = X and V = X + Y. The inverse is x = u, y = v − u, and
    ∂(x,y)/∂(u,v) = det [[1, 0], [−1, 1]] = 1.
So the joint density carries over unchanged:
    f_{U,V}(u, v) = λ²e^(−λv)  on 0 < u < v.
Notice that it does not involve u at all. That single observation is the whole of June 2026's question: for fixed v, the density is flat in u.

blocks.h: Route three: the conditional density as a ratio
blocks.body:
f(x | X + Y = s) = f_{X,Y}(x, s − x) / f_{X+Y}(s).
With two independent exponentials the numerator is λ²e^(−λs) and the denominator is the Gamma(2, λ) density s λ²e^(−λs), so the ratio is 1/s on 0 < x < s:
    X | X + Y = s  ~  Uniform(0, s),  and  E(X | X + Y = s) = s/2.
Both the result and that expectation are practice variants.

blocks.h: The exponential–Gamma facts worth knowing cold
blocks.body:
Sum of n iid exponential(λ)  → Gamma(n, λ), mean n/λ, variance n/λ².
Minimum of n iid exponential(λ) → exponential(nλ), mean 1/(nλ).
X/(X + Y) for two iid           → Uniform(0, 1), the scale-free version of the main result.
2λX for one exponential(λ)      → χ² with 2 degrees of freedom.
The last is a scaling: λX ~ exponential(1) = Gamma(1, 1), and doubling gives Gamma(1, scale 2) = χ²₂. Confirmed by simulation: mean 1.998 and variance 4.005 against the χ²₂ values 2 and 4, with KS p = 0.101.

Minimum or maximum → cdf method, one line. A conditional given a sum → the ratio, also one line. Anything else, or a genuinely two-dimensional answer → the Jacobian. The Jacobian is the general tool and the other two are shortcuts worth having, because an exam question on a minimum should not take a page.

ask.q: The transformed joint density λ²e^(−λv) does not involve u at all. Which of this lesson's results follow from that one observation?
ask.nudge: A density that is constant in u, on the region 0 < u < v, is what kind of distribution for u given v?

scenes.title: Worked in full — June 2026, Q25
scenes.objective: Derive the conditional distribution and see why the rate disappears.

ask.q: The answer Uniform(0, 2) contains no λ. Where did it cancel?
ask.nudge: Write out the numerator and the denominator of the ratio and compare their exponential factors.

scenes.problem: Let X and Y be independent, each exponential with parameter λ. Find the conditional distribution of X given X + Y = 2.

steps.say: Write the joint density and notice its structure.
steps.math: f(x, y) = λe^(−λx) · λe^(−λy) = λ² e^(−λ(x+y)),  x, y > 0
steps.why: It depends on x and y only through their SUM. So along any line x + y = constant the density is constant — which already tells you the answer before any division.

steps.say: Get the density of the sum.
steps.math:
X + Y ~ Gamma(2, λ)
f_{X+Y}(s) = λ² s e^(−λs),  s > 0
steps.why: The sum of two independent exponential(λ) variables is Gamma(2, λ). This is the distribution the marked answer gave — correct for X + Y, but the question asked about X.

steps.say: Form the conditional density as a ratio.
steps.math:
f(x | X + Y = s) = f(x, s − x) / f_{X+Y}(s)
                 = λ² e^(−λs) / (λ² s e^(−λs))
                 = 1/s,     for 0 < x < s
steps.why: Both λ² factors cancel and both e^(−λs) factors cancel — answering the question above. What is left is 1/s, a constant in x, which is the density of a uniform distribution on (0, s).

steps.say: Name the distribution and substitute s = 2.
steps.math:
X | X + Y = s  ~  Uniform(0, s)
at s = 2:  Uniform(0, 2)
⟹ option C
steps.why: Option D, Gamma(2, λ), is the sum's distribution; option A is an exponential, which has unbounded support and so cannot be right for a variable confined to (0, 2); option B is a Beta with the parameters misused.

steps.math:
600,000 pairs at λ = 1.5, keeping those with |X+Y − 2| < 0.02 (5,397 draws)
sample mean 1.0051   (Uniform(0,2) mean 1)
sample sd   0.5772   (2/√12 = 0.5774)
deciles 0.207, 0.499, 1.009, 1.511, 1.792 against 0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 1.8
Kolmogorov–Smirnov p = 0.230
steps.why: Flat across the whole interval, not merely right on average — the quantiles match throughout. A mean of 1 alone would also be consistent with a symmetric distribution peaked at the centre, so the quantiles are the check that matters.

scenes.after: Two things to carry. The joint density of independent exponentials depends only on the sum, which makes every conditional-given-the-sum question in this family uniform. And the answer has no λ in it, which is worth noticing as a check: if your answer to a 'given the total' question still contains the rate, something has not cancelled that should have.

scenes.title: Pause and recall
scenes.objective: Retrieve the main results before the variations.

items.q: What is the conditional distribution of X given X + Y = s, for iid exponentials?
items.a: Uniform(0, s), with mean s/2. The rate λ cancels.

items.q: What is the distribution of the sum of n iid exponential(λ)?
items.a: Gamma(n, λ), with mean n/λ and variance n/λ².

items.q: And the minimum of n iid exponential(λ)?
items.a: Exponential with rate nλ, so mean 1/(nλ).

items.q: What is the Jacobian of the map (x, y) → (u, v) = (x, x + y)?
items.a: 1 — so the joint density transfers unchanged.

items.q: What is the distribution of X/(X + Y) for two iid exponentials?

scenes.title: Your turn — three transformations of the same pair
scenes.objective: Apply the three routes to the same exponential pair.
scenes.problem: X and Y are independent exponential(λ). Work out three more facts about them.

blank.prompt: Give the distribution of X/(X + Y).
blank.hint: You know X | X+Y = s is Uniform(0, s). What does dividing by s do?

steps.why: Given X + Y = s, X is Uniform(0, s), so X/s is Uniform(0, 1) — and that holds for EVERY s, so the unconditional distribution of X/(X+Y) is Uniform(0,1) too. Simulated: mean 0.49992 against 0.5, variance 0.08341 against 1/12 = 0.08333, KS p = 0.890.

blank.hint: The mean of a uniform distribution on (0, s).

steps.why: s/2, by symmetry of the uniform. The traps offered in the variant are s, 1/λ and s/λ — note that the correct answer contains no λ, consistent with the cancellation in section 5. This is also what the tower property demands: E(E(X | X+Y)) = E((X+Y)/2) = (2/λ)/2 = 1/λ = E(X) ✓.

blank.prompt: If X ~ exponential(λ), what is the distribution of 2λX?
blank.hint: First find the distribution of λX, then of twice that.

steps.why: λX ~ exponential(1) = Gamma(1, 1), and multiplying by 2 gives Gamma(shape 1, scale 2), which is exactly χ² with 2 degrees of freedom. Simulated: mean 1.9984 and variance 4.0045 against the χ²₂ values 2 and 4, KS p = 0.101.

steps.say: Finally the minimum, by the cdf route.

blank.prompt: Give the distribution of min(X₁, …, Xₙ) for iid exponential(λ).
blank.hint: P(min > t) = P(all > t), and each survival is e^(−λt).

steps.why: P(min > t) = (e^(−λt))ⁿ = e^(−nλt), which is the survival function of an exponential with rate nλ. The trap is exponential(λ/n), which would make the minimum SLOWER than one component — the opposite of the truth. Simulated at λ = 1.5: mean 0.2217 for n = 3 against 0.2222.

scenes.after: Notice that three of the four were one line each, once the right route was chosen: the ratio followed from the conditional, the expectation from the uniform's symmetry, and the minimum from a product of survival functions. Only the scaling needed any manipulation, and that was a change of units. The Jacobian machinery is the fallback, not the first move.

scenes.title: Conditioning on a total, in three families
scenes.objective: See the same structure in Poisson counts and binomial counts.

blocks.body: Conditioning on a total removes the scale of the process and leaves only the proportions. It happened in the exponential case — the rate λ cancelled — and it happens for counts too, where the rates or probabilities cancel and leave a distribution governed purely by relative sizes.

blocks.h: Poisson counts given their total: binomial
blocks.body:
If N₁ ~ Poisson(μ₁) and N₂ ~ Poisson(μ₂) are independent, then
    N₁ | N₁ + N₂ = k  ~  Binomial(k, μ₁/(μ₁ + μ₂)).
For Poisson processes with rates λ and 2λ the proportion is λ/(3λ) = 1/3 — the λ cancels. So with k = 4,
    P(N₁ = 1 | total = 4) = C(4,1)(1/3)(2/3)³ = 32/81 = 0.39506,
a practice variant. Simulated over 101,098 qualifying draws: 0.39459.

blocks.h: Binomial counts given their total: hypergeometric
blocks.body:
If X ~ Binomial(m, p) and Y ~ Binomial(n, p) are independent with the SAME p, then
    X | X + Y = k  ~  Hypergeometric(m + n, m, k),
so P(X = j) = C(m,j)C(n,k−j)/C(m+n,k) — free of p entirely. A practice variant asks exactly this. Checked at m = 6, n = 4, k = 3: the empirical probabilities 0.0327, 0.3003, 0.4991, 0.1680 against the exact 0.0333, 0.3000, 0.5000, 0.1667.

blocks.h: Why p and λ always cancel
blocks.body: In each case the conditional probability is a ratio in which the parameter appears to the same power in numerator and denominator. That is not a coincidence: conditioning on the total fixes the quantity the parameter controls, so nothing is left for it to influence. It is also why these conditional distributions are the basis of EXACT tests — Fisher's exact test is precisely the hypergeometric conditional above, and it needs no estimate of p.

The continuous analogue of the Poisson result is the one from section 5: given that exactly one event of a Poisson process occurred in an interval, its position is uniform over the interval. Given that k occurred, their positions behave like k independent uniforms, sorted — which is the order statistics of lesson 1.1, with expected positions at j/(k+1).

ask.q: Fisher's exact test uses the hypergeometric conditional distribution. Why is it an advantage that p cancels?
ask.nudge: What would you otherwise have to do about an unknown nuisance parameter before computing a p-value?

scenes.title: On your own — splitting a Poisson stream
scenes.objective: Apply the conditioning result to counts, with numbers.
scenes.problem: Two independent Poisson processes have rates λ and 2λ. (a) Given that 4 events occurred in total, name the conditional distribution of the number from the first process. (b) Find P(N₁ = 1 | N₁ + N₂ = 4). (c) Find E(N₁ | N₁ + N₂ = 4). (d) Does any of this depend on λ, or on the length of the observation period?
hints: For (a), the conditional distribution is binomial with the proportion of the total rate.
For (b), use the binomial pmf with that proportion.
For (d), write the proportion in terms of λ and simplify.
scenes.answer: (a) Binomial(4, 1/3). (b) 32/81 = 0.39506. (c) 4/3. (d) No — λ and the period both cancel out of the proportion.
scenes.check: Part (d) is the point of the exercise. The proportion is λt/(λt + 2λt) = 1/3 whatever λ and whatever t, so the answer depends only on the RATIO of the rates. That is why conditioning on a total is such a useful device: it eliminates the nuisance parameter. Simulated over 101,098 qualifying draws, P(N₁ = 1 | total = 4) came to 0.39459 against the exact 0.39506.

scenario.teaser: Two call centres share a queue and a manager wants to know each one's share of a busy hour.
scenario.title: Conditioning away the thing you do not know
body: Two support teams handle calls from a common stream. Team A handles roughly half as many as Team B, and in a given hour 4 calls arrived in total. The manager wants the probability that exactly one of them went to Team A.

The arrival rate is not known — it varies by day, by season and by how the product is behaving — and estimating it would need historical data the manager does not have to hand. It turns out not to matter.

Modelling the two streams as independent Poisson processes with rates λ and 2λ, the conditional distribution of Team A's count given the total of 4 is Binomial(4, 1/3). The λ cancels, because conditioning on the total has already fixed the only thing λ governs: how many calls there were. What remains is purely the split, and the split depends only on the ratio of the rates.
So P(exactly one to Team A) = C(4,1)(1/3)(2/3)³ = 32/81 ≈ 0.395, and the expected count is 4/3. Neither figure requires knowing the arrival rate or even the length of the observation window.

This is the same device that makes several exact tests work. Fisher's exact test conditions on the margins of a 2×2 table precisely so that the unknown common success probability drops out, leaving a hypergeometric calculation that needs no estimate. Conditioning on a sufficient statistic for the nuisance parameter is the general principle, and lesson 4.1's material is where it comes from.

The caution is that the RATIO still has to be known or assumed. Here 'A handles half as many as B' supplied it. Had the manager known only that the two teams differ, nothing could be computed — conditioning removes one unknown, not all of them.
scenario.q: Why can this be answered without knowing the arrival rate, and what would still have to be known?
scenario.answer: Because conditioning on the total of 4 fixes the quantity the rate controls — how many calls arrived — so the rate has nothing left to influence and cancels from the conditional distribution. What survives is the proportion λ/(λ + 2λ) = 1/3, which depends only on the RATIO of the two rates, not on their size or on the length of the window. So the ratio is exactly what must still be known: the statement that Team A handles half as many as Team B supplies it, and without some such assumption the split would be uncomputable. This is the same reason Fisher's exact test conditions on the margins — to eliminate a nuisance parameter while retaining what the question needs.

solution.math:
N₁ ~ Poisson(λt), N₂ ~ Poisson(2λt), independent
N₁ | N₁ + N₂ = k ~ Binomial(k, λt/(λt + 2λt)) = Binomial(k, 1/3)
with k = 4:  Binomial(4, 1/3)
solution.why: The standard result for splitting a Poisson total. The proportion is the first rate over the total rate.
Simulated over 101,098 qualifying draws as 0.39459 — agreement to three decimals.
The binomial mean. Sensible: of four calls, the team taking a third of the traffic should get about 1.3 of them.

solution.math:
proportion = λt/(λt + 2λt) = 1/3
λ cancels; t cancels
solution.why: No dependence on the rate or the period — only on the RATIO 1:2. That is the device: conditioning on the total eliminates the nuisance parameter, which is exactly why exact tests condition on margins.

scenes.title: Six statements — verdict on each before you look
scenes.objective: Rule on the claims the variants on this topic are built from.
scenes.intro: Decide true or false on all six before revealing any.

items.claim: For iid exponentials, X | X + Y = s is Uniform(0, s).
items.why: True, and the rate cancels completely. The joint density λ²e^(−λ(x+y)) depends on x and y only through the sum, so it is constant along any line of fixed sum. Verified by simulation: KS p = 0.230 against Uniform(0,2).

items.claim: The sum of n iid exponential(λ) variables is exponential with rate nλ.
items.why: False — that is the MINIMUM. The sum is Gamma(n, λ) with mean n/λ, which GROWS with n, whereas exponential(nλ) has mean 1/(nλ), which shrinks. The two results are easy to swap and point in opposite directions.

items.claim: The minimum of n iid exponential(λ) is exponential with rate nλ.
items.why: True. P(min > t) = (e^(−λt))ⁿ = e^(−nλt). The rate multiplies by n, so the minimum arrives n times sooner on average — mean 1/(nλ). Answering exponential(λ/n) makes it slower, which is the wrong direction.

items.claim: X/(X + Y) for two iid exponentials is Uniform(0, 1).
items.why: True, and it follows from the main result: given X + Y = s, X is Uniform(0, s), so X/s is Uniform(0,1) for every s. Simulated mean 0.49992 and variance 0.08341 against 0.5 and 1/12.

items.claim: If X ~ Binomial(m, p) and Y ~ Binomial(n, p) independently, then X | X + Y = k is binomial.
items.why: False — it is HYPERGEOMETRIC, with P(X = j) = C(m,j)C(n,k−j)/C(m+n,k), free of p. Conditioning on the total makes the problem one of drawing k items without replacement from m + n. This is the distribution behind Fisher's exact test.

items.claim: E(X | X + Y = s) equals 1/λ for iid exponentials.
items.why: False: it is s/2. 1/λ is the UNCONDITIONAL mean E(X). The conditional expectation must depend on s — it is half of whatever total was observed — and containing λ would contradict the cancellation that makes the conditional uniform.

scenes.title: On your own — six quick ones
scenes.objective: Apply the standard transformations at speed.
scenes.problem: Let X, Y, X₁, …, Xₙ be independent exponential(λ). Give: (a) the distribution of X + Y; (b) the distribution of min(X₁, …, X₅) and its mean when λ = 2; (c) E(X | X + Y = 6); (d) the distribution of 2λX; (e) P(T > 6 | T > 4) for T exponential with rate 2; (f) the Jacobian of (x, y) → (x, x + y).
hints: For (b), the rate multiplies by the number of variables.
For (c), the conditional is uniform on the interval.
For (e), use memorylessness rather than integrating.
scenes.answer: (a) Gamma(2, λ). (b) Exponential(5λ) = exponential(10), mean 0.1. (c) 3. (d) χ² with 2 df. (e) e^(−4) = 0.018316. (f) 1.
scenes.check: Part (e) is worth doing carefully. Memorylessness gives P(T > 6 | T > 4) = P(T > 2) = e^(−2×2) = e^(−4) = 0.018316. Note the rate is 2, so the exponent is 2 × 2 = 4, not 2 — and the answer is NOT e^(−6) or e^(−2). A direct simulation of this is a poor check: with 600,000 draws only 205 exceed 4, so the conditional estimate has an enormous standard error. Simulating the SHIFTED variable instead, over four million draws, gave 0.018388 against the exact 0.018316.

solution.math: X + Y ~ Gamma(2, λ),  mean 2/λ, variance 2/λ²
solution.why: The shape parameter counts the exponentials. This is the distribution the exam's marked answer gave for a question about X.

solution.math:
P(min > t) = e^(−5λt) ⟹ exponential(5λ)
at λ = 2: rate 10, mean 1/10 = 0.1
solution.why: Five independent components in series fail five times sooner on average than one.
Half the total, with no λ anywhere.

solution.math:
λX ~ exponential(1) = Gamma(1,1)
2λX ~ Gamma(shape 1, scale 2) = χ²₂
solution.why: Simulated mean 1.998 and variance 4.005 against the χ²₂ values 2 and 4.
The elapsed four minutes are forgotten entirely. The exponent uses the rate times the REMAINING time.
Unit Jacobian, so the joint density carries over with no scaling factor — which is what keeps the main derivation to three lines.

scenes.title: Where transformations do the work
scenes.objective: Recognise the method across the rest of the syllabus.

blocks.body: Every classical sampling distribution is a transformation: chi-square is a sum of squared normals, t is a normal over the root of an independent chi-square, F is a ratio of chi-squares. The Jacobian method is how each density is derived, and 2λX ~ χ²₂ from this lesson is the simplest instance.

blocks.h: In Bayesian work and the Beta
blocks.body: If U ~ Gamma(a, λ) and V ~ Gamma(b, λ) independently, then U/(U+V) ~ Beta(a, b), and this lesson's X/(X+Y) ~ Uniform(0,1) is the case a = b = 1, since Beta(1,1) IS the uniform. The same construction gives the Dirichlet in several dimensions, which is the conjugate prior for the multinomial.

Fisher's exact test conditions a 2×2 table on its margins, which turns the two binomials into the hypergeometric of section 8 and removes the unknown common probability. Conditioning on a sufficient statistic to eliminate a nuisance parameter is the general device, and it comes from the sufficiency material of topic 4.1.

The inverse-transform method generates a variable from any continuous distribution as F⁻¹(U) with U uniform — a transformation whose correctness is the probability integral transform of lesson 1.13. For the exponential it gives −ln(U)/λ, which is the standard generator.

Nothing in this topic is new probability; it is bookkeeping about densities under a change of variables, plus the two shortcuts for minima and for conditioning on a sum. Recognising which of the three routes a question wants is most of the work, and the choice is usually settled by the form of the thing being asked about.

ask.q: U/(U+V) is Beta(a, b) for independent Gammas with the same rate. Which values of a and b give this lesson's Uniform(0,1) result, and why?
ask.nudge: An exponential is a Gamma with shape 1. And Beta(1,1) is which distribution?

scenes.title: Second recall — the parts most likely to fade
scenes.objective: Retrieve the conditioning results and the directions.

items.q: Sum versus minimum of n iid exponential(λ): which is Gamma and which is exponential?
items.a: The sum is Gamma(n, λ) with mean n/λ; the minimum is exponential(nλ) with mean 1/(nλ).

items.q: Two independent Poissons given their total: what distribution, with what parameter?
items.a: Binomial(k, μ₁/(μ₁+μ₂)) — for rates λ and 2λ that is Binomial(k, 1/3).

items.q: Two independent binomials with the same p, given their total?
items.a: Hypergeometric, free of p — the basis of Fisher's exact test.

items.q: P(N₁ = 1 | N₁ + N₂ = 4) for rates λ and 2λ?
What is the Jacobian of (x, y) → (x, x + y), and why does it matter?
items.a: 1, so the joint density transfers unchanged — which keeps the main derivation short.

items.q: For T exponential with rate 2, what is P(T > 6 | T > 4)?

scenes.title: What you should now be able to do unaided
scenes.objective: Close the loop before the mastery test.
body: Choose between the cdf route, the Jacobian route and the conditional-ratio route from the form of the question.
Compute the Jacobian of (x, y) → (x, x + y) and say why it is 1.
Derive that X | X + Y = s is Uniform(0, s) and explain where λ cancels.
Give the sum as Gamma(n, λ) and the minimum as exponential(nλ), without swapping them.
Derive X/(X + Y) ~ Uniform(0,1) and 2λX ~ χ²₂.
Condition Poisson counts on their total to get a binomial, and binomial counts to get a hypergeometric.
Use memorylessness rather than integrating, and get the exponent right.

scenes.title: The Jacobian theorem, and the Beta from two Gammas
scenes.objective: See the general statement and the derivation the topic is really about.

blocks.body:
Let (U, V) = g(X, Y) be one-to-one and continuously differentiable with non-vanishing Jacobian on the support. Then
    f_{U,V}(u, v) = f_{X,Y}(h₁(u,v), h₂(u,v)) · |J|,   J = det ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v),
where h is the inverse map. In n dimensions the statement is identical with an n × n determinant. If g is not one-to-one, split the support into pieces on which it is and add the contributions.

A density is probability per unit area, so if the map stretches a small region by a factor, the density must shrink by the same factor for the probability to be preserved. The determinant of the derivative matrix is precisely the local area-scaling factor, and the absolute value is taken because orientation is irrelevant to area.

blocks.h: The Beta from two Gammas, derived
blocks.body:
Let U ~ Gamma(a, λ) and V ~ Gamma(b, λ) be independent and set
    R = U/(U+V),  S = U + V.
The inverse is u = rs, v = s(1−r), with Jacobian det [[s, r], [−s, 1−r]] = s. Substituting the Gamma densities, the joint density factorises into a function of r times a function of s:
    f(r, s) ∝ r^(a−1)(1−r)^(b−1) · s^(a+b−1)e^(−λs).
So R ~ Beta(a, b) and S ~ Gamma(a+b, λ), and they are INDEPENDENT — which is the striking part. With a = b = 1 the exponential case gives R ~ Beta(1,1) = Uniform(0,1), this lesson's result.

The sum carries all the information about the scale and the ratio carries all the information about the split, and the two are independent. That is why conditioning on the sum leaves a distribution free of λ: the ratio never knew about λ in the first place. It is also the construction behind the Dirichlet distribution and behind the standard algorithm for generating Beta variables from Gammas.

blocks.h: A caution about the one-to-one requirement
blocks.body: For Y = X² with X symmetric about 0, the map is two-to-one and the naive formula fails. Splitting into x > 0 and x < 0 and adding gives f_Y(y) = [f_X(√y) + f_X(−√y)]/(2√y), which for a standard normal is the chi-square with one degree of freedom. Forgetting the second branch halves the answer, and this is the most common way the method is misapplied.

ask.q: In the Beta–Gamma derivation the joint density factorised into a function of r times a function of s. What does that factorisation prove?
ask.nudge: A joint density that factors into a function of each variable separately says what about those variables?

scenes.objective: Demonstrate it independently, on questions you have not seen.
